title: Starting a Business
description: Ten calm texts about starting and running a small business: a business plan, a bakery's first year, family money or a bank loan, a founder who failed and tried again, pricing, a first employee, a cooperative bookstore, work and family, a coffee roaster and a shop sign.

lessons.title: Writing a Business Plan
lessons.summary: A math teacher who wants to become a private tutor writes an honest business plan before she leaves her job.
lessons.text:
For almost a year, Maya Ortiz contemplated leaving her job as a high school math teacher. What she contemplated was not leaving teaching altogether, but teaching in a different way: as a private tutor with a small business of her own. First, however, she wrote a business plan.

A business plan, Maya learned, is less a document for the bank than a tool for thinking. It forces you to answer hard questions in writing. Who are your customers? Why would they choose you? How long will it take before the business pays for itself?

Maya began with her niche. A niche is a small, clearly defined part of a market, and new businesses are often advised to find one rather than try to serve everyone. Several large tutoring companies in her city already offered help in every subject. Maya could not compete with them on size, so she chose a narrow niche: geometry and early algebra for students aged twelve to fifteen. She knew from the classroom that geometry was where many students first decided they were "bad at math."

Next, she described the service. Each student would see the same tutor every week, and every session would end with a short quiz of five questions, so that parents could see progress. A longer quiz at the free first meeting would show the gaps in each student's knowledge.

The money section was the hardest to write honestly. It is tempting, in a business plan, to exaggerate. Owners often exaggerate how many customers they will have, partly to impress others and partly to convince themselves. Maya decided not to exaggerate anything. Instead, she wrote three versions of her first year: a cautious one, a likely one and a hopeful one. For each, she estimated the likelihood that it would come true. She judged the likelihood of the cautious version to be high, and that of the hopeful one to be low.

She also listed her constraints. A constraint is anything that limits what you can do. Her savings would cover only eight months of living costs. Most students were free only after school, so she could not work more than about twenty-five hours a week. That was the biggest constraint of all.

Finally, she added a section that most guides called optional: plans for the future. Optional or not, she found it useful. In it, she described a service she might offer later, reading and literacy support for younger children. Many students who struggle with word problems in math, she had noticed, actually have trouble with literacy, not with numbers.

A friend who ran a small business read the plan and asked one question: "Does this still work if the cautious version comes true?" It did. A month later, Maya resigned.

Questions:
What had Maya contemplated for almost a year?
She had contemplated leaving her teaching job to work as a private tutor with a business of her own.
Why did Maya choose a narrow niche?
She could not compete with the large tutoring companies on size, so she chose geometry and early algebra.
Why did Maya write three versions of her first year?
She did not want to exaggerate, so she wrote three versions and estimated the likelihood of each.
What was her biggest constraint?
Students were free only after school, so she could not work more than about twenty-five hours a week.
What did she describe in the optional section?
She described a future literacy service for younger children.

lessons.title: A Bakery's First Year
lessons.summary: A baker looks back on the first year of her small bakery and the lessons it taught her.
lessons.text:
My name is Rosa, and one year ago this week, I unlocked the door of my small bakery for the first time. I had baked at home all my life, but I had never run a business. Here, for anyone thinking of doing the same, is what my first year taught me.

The first month was terribly hard. I arrived at four in the morning, mixed the batter for the muffins, shaped the bread, and was still behind when the first customers came at seven. I was terribly tired, and I burned my hands twice in the first week because I kept reaching into the oven with a thin kitchen towel. After that, I bought two thick oven mitts and hung them on a hook next to the oven, and I have not been burned since. The mitts taught me a simple lesson: buy the right tools before you need them.

I also learned to plan the mornings. Muffin batter can be made the night before and kept cold, so I began to prepare it in the evening. In the morning, I only had to put paper liners in the pans, fill each liner with batter and bake. The liners cost money, but they saved me twenty minutes of washing pans every day.

The second lesson was about appetite: not mine, but my customers'. I had planned to sell what I loved to bake, such as fancy cakes. The town's appetite, however, was for simpler things: good bread, coffee and something sweet to eat on the way to work. Within two months, the cheese danish had become my best seller. A danish takes time to make, because the dough is folded with butter many times, but people came back for it every morning.

The third lesson was about the other shops on my street. Next door is a butcher, Mr. Kowalski, who has worked on this street for thirty years. In my first week, the butcher brought me a cup of coffee and a list of every supplier in town who could be trusted. Later, when my fridge broke on a hot day in July, he kept my butter in his cold room until it was repaired. Now I bake an extra loaf for the butcher every Friday.

Not everything went well. The kitchen was messy for months, because I never had time to organize it, and a messy kitchen is a slow kitchen. In August, I finally closed for two days and put everything in order, and the mornings became calmer at once.

Will the business flourish? It is too early to say. A small shop needs a few years, not one, to flourish. But we are paying our bills, and on Saturdays the line reaches the corner. For a first year, that is enough.

Questions:
Why did Rosa buy oven mitts?
She burned her hands twice in the first week because she used a thin kitchen towel.
Why did she start making the muffin batter in the evening?
Batter can be kept cold overnight, so in the morning she only had to fill the paper liners and bake.
What was the town's appetite for?
The town's appetite was for simple things: good bread, coffee and something sweet.
How did the butcher help her?
He gave her a list of trusted suppliers and kept her butter cold when her fridge broke.
Why was a messy kitchen a problem?
A messy kitchen was a slow kitchen.

lessons.title: Family Money or a Bank Loan?
lessons.summary: A short guide compares borrowing from a relative with borrowing from a bank, using the case of a man who wants to open a bicycle shop.
lessons.text:
Sooner or later, almost everyone who starts a small business faces the same question: where will the money come from? For many owners there are two realistic answers, a bank or the family. This short guide compares them.

Consider a typical case. Sam wants to open a bicycle repair shop and needs 20,000 dollars. His aunt has recently inherited some money from her father, and she has offered to lend him the whole amount. His bank will also consider a loan, albeit at 9 percent interest and only if Sam can show a detailed business plan.

The case for family money is easy to see. A relative usually asks for little or no interest, needs no long application and will not reject Sam because his business is new.

The case for the bank is just as strong, albeit less warm. A bank loan comes with a written contract that states the amount, the interest, the date of each payment and what happens if a payment is missed. The contract binds both sides: it binds the bank as well as Sam, so the bank cannot suddenly ask for its money back. Banks are also watched by government regulators, whose job is to make sure that lenders treat customers fairly. If Sam believes the bank has broken the rules, he can complain to a regulator. If his aunt changes her mind, there is no regulator to call.

What the bank offers, in other words, is transparency and accountability. Transparency means that everyone can see the rules from the beginning. Accountability means that each side must answer for what it does. Family loans often have neither. Many rest on a verbal agreement made over dinner, and a verbal agreement is easy to remember differently a few years later. Did the aunt say "pay me back when you can," or "within two years"? Without a written record, the question can damage a relationship that matters far more than any shop.

The sensible answer, many advisers say, is to treat family money with the same care as bank money. Sam and his aunt should write down the amount, the payments and the dates, and both should sign. This simple step is a safeguard for both of them, and a safeguard for the rest of the family too. If a cousin later raises a query about the loan, the paper answers the query.

Finally, Sam should be honest about the risk. The money his aunt inherited may be most of her savings, and her prosperity in old age may depend on getting it back. A bank can survive a lost loan; a retired aunt may not. Whoever lends the money, an owner's prosperity should never come at the expense of someone he loves.

Questions:
Where can Sam borrow the money for his shop?
He can borrow it from his aunt, who recently inherited some money, or from his bank, albeit at 9 percent interest.
Why does the bank contract bind both sides?
It states the rules for the bank as well as for Sam, so neither side can change them suddenly.
What do bank regulators do?
They make sure that lenders treat customers fairly.
Why can a verbal agreement cause problems?
People can remember a verbal agreement differently years later, and that can damage a relationship.
What safeguard do the advisers suggest?
They suggest writing the loan down and having both people sign it.

lessons.title: The Boxer Who Opened Two Gyms
lessons.summary: A profile of a former boxer whose first gym failed and whose second, planned more carefully, succeeded.
lessons.text:
Daniel Reyes was a boxer for eleven years. He was never a champion, but he was a good, persistent boxer who trained every day and rarely lost by much. When he retired at thirty-two, he did what many former athletes dream of doing. He opened his own gym.

The first gym lasted less than two years. Looking back, Daniel can explain exactly why it failed. He chose a large space in an expensive part of the city because it looked impressive. He taught every class himself, although he was a better boxer than teacher. Most of all, he had no money in reserve. When the road outside was closed for repairs for four months, new members stopped coming, and his savings were soon gone.

People who study small businesses have a useful term for this: business mortality. The mortality rate of new businesses is the share that close within a given number of years. In the United States, roughly one in five new businesses closes within its first year. Daniel did not know these numbers when he started. "I thought hard work was enough," he says. "Hard work is necessary, but it isn't enough."

The aftermath of closing was, in his words, "the worst year of my life." He owed money to two suppliers, and he worked nights in a warehouse. He describes that time as a lone misery: lone because he stopped calling his friends, and misery because he believed he had failed in public. Some people harden in a period like that. They harden into anger and blame the road, the economy or their customers. Daniel was close to that, but his sister refused to let him hide. "She came every Sunday," he says, "and asked me what I had learned that week."

Slowly, the answers became a plan. In the aftermath of the first gym, he wrote down every mistake and what it had cost. Then he did what persistent people do: he decided to persist, but differently. His second gym, opened three years later, is in a former garage in a cheaper neighborhood, with second-hand equipment. Before opening, he saved enough to cover six months of costs, and he hired a coach who teaches beginners better than he does.

The new gym has now been open for four years, and it makes a modest profit. Daniel is still amazed by how much of his success comes from boring decisions. "People are amazed when I tell them the secret was a cheap lease," he says with a smile.

Last month, he held a small farewell party for the warehouse job he had kept part-time until then. At the farewell, his sister gave a short speech. "He learned to persist," she said, "and to change at the same time."

Questions:
What did Daniel do before he opened a gym?
He was a boxer for eleven years.
Why did the first gym fail?
The space was expensive, he taught every class himself, and he had no money in reserve when the road outside was closed.
What does business mortality mean?
It means the share of new businesses that close within a given number of years.
How does Daniel describe the aftermath of closing?
He describes it as a lone misery and the worst year of his life.
How is the second gym different?
It is in a cheaper former garage, he saved six months of costs before opening, and another coach teaches beginners.

lessons.title: Pricing a Wool Scarf
lessons.summary: A woman who knits scarves learns, step by step, how to set an honest price for her work.
lessons.text:
When Hannah Berg began selling her hand-knit wool scarves at a weekend market, she priced them the way many beginners do. She looked at what similar scarves cost in shops, chose a number slightly below it and hoped for the best. She charged 40 dollars a scarf. After a winter of good sales, she had almost no money to show for it.

Pricing, as Hannah learned, begins with costs, not with competitors. The wool for one scarf cost her about 20 dollars, because she used a soft local wool from a small farm. A small card would accompany each scarf, telling the story of the farm, and she wanted that card to accompany every scarf she sold.

Then there was time, which beginners often forget to count. A scarf took her about five hours to knit. Even at 15 dollars an hour, those hours were worth 75 dollars. An honest cost for one scarf was close to 100 dollars. At 40 dollars, she had been paying her customers to take her work.

The second step is to understand the market. Hannah had no monopoly. A monopoly exists when a single seller controls a product, so that buyers have nowhere else to go. At her market alone, four other sellers offered knitted goods, and online there were thousands. Without a monopoly, she had to give buyers a reason to pay more, and her reason was the local wool and the story on the card.

Some sellers try to penetrate a market with a very low price: they lure buyers with cheap goods and plan to raise prices later. This can work for large companies with money in reserve. For one person working alone, it is dangerous, because the buyers you lure with low prices are often the first to leave when prices rise. Hannah decided not to penetrate the whole market. She would sell to the smaller group of people who valued what she made.

So she raised the price, a notch at a time: to 60 dollars in the spring, and to 90 the following fall. Each notch lost her a few customers, but her income rose. She also began to sell from her own website, which let her bypass the market fee and reach buyers in other states. She never wanted to bypass the market completely, though; she enjoys the weekends there.

She also learned to plan for surplus. At the end of each season, some scarves remained. Rather than cutting the price of this surplus, which might induce regular customers to wait for a sale, she gave the surplus scarves to a winter coat drive. Discounts, she believes, induce the wrong habit in buyers.

Hannah still reviews her prices continually. "Pricing is not a decision you make once," she says. "You make it continually, for as long as the business exists."

Questions:
How did Hannah first choose her price?
She looked at prices in shops and chose a number slightly below them.
What did the card that accompanies each scarf tell?
It told the story of the farm where the wool came from.
Why could Hannah not name any price she liked?
She had no monopoly, because many other sellers offered knitted goods.
Why is it dangerous for one person to lure buyers with very low prices?
The buyers she lures with low prices are often the first to leave when prices rise.
What did Hannah do with her surplus scarves?
She gave them to a winter coat drive instead of cutting their price.

lessons.title: The First Employee
lessons.summary: The owner of a skate shop plans, step by step, how to hire and welcome his first employee.
lessons.text:
For three years, Leo Park ran his skate shop alone. He sold boards and shoes, repaired wheels in the back room, and did the ordering and the accounts at night. By the third summer, he was tired in a way that sleep no longer fixed, and he understood that the shop needed a second person.

Hiring a first employee is a large step for any small business, and Leo approached it as a process with several stages.

First, he wrote down every task in the shop and decided which tasks he would assign to the new person. He did not want to assign only the jobs he disliked, because that would make the work dull and lead to high turnover. Turnover is the rate at which employees leave and must be replaced. Every time a worker leaves, the owner must find and train someone new, so high turnover costs time and money. Leo decided to assign a fair mix: work with customers, some repairs and the shop's social media.

Second, he learned the rules. There were forms to fill out, taxes to pay and insurance to buy. He chose an automated payroll service, which calculates wages and taxes and pays them on the right day. The automated service cost 30 dollars a month and saved him from many mistakes. He also learned that the law forbids employers to choose workers because of their religion or age, so questions about such things do not belong in an interview. Leo had not known that; now he knew what the law forbids.

Third, he looked for the right person. He wanted an insider: someone who could skate, knew the local parks and could talk to customers in their own language. The best candidate was Nina, who had worked in a sporting goods store and had started to skate when she was ten. In the interview, she asked as many questions as Leo did, which he took as a good sign.

Finally, he planned her first week. On Monday, Nina simply followed him around. On Tuesday, she handled sales while he watched. By Friday, she was repairing wheels on her own. Leo also made the week enjoyable on purpose. He took her to lunch, introduced her to the regular customers and let her choose the music.

The results came quickly. Nina understood the young customers who arrived after school with boards tied to their backpacks, and she suggested a backpack with a built-in board holder that soon became a best seller. As an insider, she also knew which local riders might teach weekend classes.

A year later, Nina is still there. Leo works fewer hours, the shop has had no turnover at all, and the work is more enjoyable for both of them.

Questions:
Why did Leo decide to hire someone?
He was very tired after running the shop alone for three years.
What is turnover?
Turnover is the rate at which employees leave and must be replaced.
Why did Leo choose an automated payroll service?
It calculates and pays wages and taxes on time, and it saved him from many mistakes.
Why was Nina a good candidate?
She was an insider who could skate and knew the local parks, and she had worked in a sporting goods store.
How did Leo make Nina's first week enjoyable?
He took her to lunch, introduced her to the regular customers and let her choose the music.

lessons.title: A Bookstore Owned by Its Readers
lessons.summary: When a town loses its only bookstore, a group of readers opens a new one as a cooperative.
lessons.text:
When the only bookstore in the suburban town of Millbrook closed, many residents assumed that the town would simply live without one. Like many suburban towns, Millbrook was a long drive from the nearest city, and most people now bought books online. A small group of readers, however, decided to own a new store themselves, as a cooperative.

A cooperative is a business owned by the people it serves. At the Millbrook store, each member pays a one-time fee of 100 dollars. In return, members receive a discount, a vote on major decisions and a share of any profit. The store is not a charitable organization: it must pay its rent and its staff like any other shop. But it is not a typical capitalist business either, because no single owner or outside investor collects the profit.

This middle position caused long debates at the first meetings, which were held in the hall of the local Baptist church. Some members wanted to run the store on purely capitalist lines. Others wanted it to be almost charitable, with free events and very low prices. The compromise was practical. The store would aim for a small, steady profit, and part of any surplus would buy books for the town's schools. The Baptist church, which had lent its hall for free, received the first gift of books.

The members also had to decide what kind of store to be. A few argued for screens and an app. Most disagreed. They felt that what people missed was precisely the analog experience: paper, shelves and a person who could recommend a book. So the store remained analog, albeit with a simple website for orders.

The new store opened in a former shoe shop on the main street. Because one founding member uses a wheelchair, the members built a ramp at the entrance and set the shelves wide apart, so that a wheelchair can move easily between them. The ramp turned out to help parents with small children as well.

Every month, members vote for a "masterpiece of the month," an older book that they think everyone in the locality should read. Last spring, the chosen masterpiece was a novel about the end of a war, and it sold more copies than any new book.

Some people expected the larger bookstores in the region to be territorial and to see the cooperative as a threat. In fact, they have been friendly. Being territorial, one manager said, makes little sense when the real competition is online.

For many members, the store has brought a kind of liberation: liberation from the feeling that their locality could only lose its shops, never gain them. "We didn't just save a bookstore," one member said. "We showed that a town can still decide what it wants to be."

Questions:
What is a cooperative?
A cooperative is a business owned by the people it serves.
Why is the store not a charitable organization?
It must pay its rent and its staff like any other shop.
Where were the first meetings held?
They were held in the hall of the local Baptist church.
Why did the members build a ramp?
One founding member uses a wheelchair, so they built a ramp and set the shelves wide apart.
What is the "masterpiece of the month"?
It is an older book that members vote for and think everyone in the locality should read.

lessons.title: Owners, Take the Evening Off
lessons.summary: In a column, the owner of a printing shop describes how she learned to stop working at the dinner table.
lessons.text:
Last spring, my six-year-old daughter asked me a question at dinner that I have not been able to forget. I was answering an email from a supplier, with my phone in one hand and my fork in the other, when she said, "Mommy, are you at work or at home?" I laughed, put the phone down and had no good answer.

I have owned a small printing shop for nine years. Like most owners I know, I never quite leave work, because work comes with me. Modern telecommunication has made it possible to run a business from anywhere, which is wonderful, and from everywhere, which is not. Thanks to telecommunication, a customer can reach me at the dinner table, in bed or smack in the middle of my daughter's school play.

The cost is not only time. When I am always available, I am never fully rested, and a tired person has a short temper. Small things made my temper flare: a late delivery, a question from my assistant, a toy on the stairs. At work, my anger would flare and then pass. At home, it sometimes turned into something close to aggression: a raised voice, a slammed door. I am not proud of that. Aggression of that kind is rarely about the toy on the stairs; it is about being worn out.

My doctor, when I described this, did not suggest medicine. What she prescribed was simpler and, for me, harder: one evening a week with no phone at all, and a walk every day. "This is prescribed," she said, half joking, "so you have to follow it."

I followed it, and then I went further. Here are the rules I now keep, offered not as expert advice but as one owner's experience.

First, the work phone stays in a drawer from six in the evening until eight in the morning. Almost nothing in a printing shop is a real emergency.

Second, I sit down for my morning coffee. I used to drink it standing at the counter, between calls. Now I take ten minutes, sip it slowly and plan the day. To sip a coffee instead of swallowing it is a daily reminder that I am a person, not a machine.

Third, I let the business run itself for short periods. A well-organized shop can run itself for a weekend, and if it cannot, that is a problem with the organization.

None of this has hurt the business. My income is the same, my assistant makes more decisions on her own, and my temper rarely flares. Last week, smack in the middle of dinner, I heard the phone buzz in its drawer, and I let it buzz. My daughter smiled. "Mommy," she said, "you're at home."

Questions:
What did the writer's daughter ask at dinner?
She asked, "Mommy, are you at work or at home?"
How has telecommunication changed the writer's life?
It lets customers reach her anywhere and at any time, so she never quite leaves work.
What did the doctor tell the writer to do?
She prescribed one evening a week with no phone at all and a walk every day.
Why does the writer now sit down to sip her coffee?
It reminds her every day that she is a person, not a machine.
What has happened since she changed her habits?
Her income is the same, her assistant makes more decisions, and her temper rarely flares.

lessons.title: From Plantation to Cup
lessons.summary: The owner of a small coffee roasting business explains each stage of a coffee bean's journey.
lessons.text:
Five years ago, Omar Haddad turned his love of coffee into a small business. His company buys raw coffee beans, roasts them in a former car repair shop and sells them to coffee shops and home customers. When people ask him what he does, he explains the whole journey of a coffee bean, because he believes that customers who understand the process are happier to pay a fair price.

The journey begins on a plantation. Omar buys most of his beans from two family-owned coffee plantations in Guatemala. One plantation lies on the slopes of an old volcano, where the soil is rich in minerals and the nights are cool. Coffee grown on the volcano has a bright, clean taste, and Omar describes it as having a note of lime.

On the plantation, the coffee fruit is picked by hand, because the fruit on a single branch is not all ready at the same time. A tractor carries the full baskets down the hill to a mill, where the fruit is removed and the beans are dried in the sun. The family bought its first tractor only ten years ago; before that, horses carried the baskets.

Transport is the next stage, and it is where world events touch even a very small business. The dried beans travel by truck to a port and then by ship. Ships and trucks burn fuel made from petroleum, so when the price of petroleum rises, Omar's costs rise too. In one difficult year, transport costs nearly doubled.

In Omar's shop, the raw beans are green and smell like grass. He roasts them in a large machine with a shining chrome front, a turning drum and a small window through which he can watch the beans grow darker. The chrome is only decoration, he admits, but customers love to photograph it.

The beans turn yellow, then light brown, and then they crack with a sound like breaking sticks. A light roast, stopped soon after the first crack, keeps the flavors of the plantation. Roasting also produces a great deal of smoke, so the building has a powerful fan and a smoke detector in every room. A fire inspector checks each detector once a year, and Omar tests them himself every month.

The last stage happens in the customer's kitchen. For most people, Omar recommends simple drip coffee: hot water passes slowly through ground coffee in a paper filter, and the coffee falls drop by drop into a pot below. A good drip method, he says, lets the taste of the plantation come through, including that note of lime.

When Omar explains all this, customers often look at their cup differently. In a single sip, they are tasting the work of many people in many places.

Questions:
Where does Omar buy most of his beans?
He buys them from two family-owned plantations in Guatemala.
What is special about the coffee from the volcano?
It has a bright, clean taste with a note of lime.
Why does the price of petroleum matter to Omar?
Ships and trucks burn fuel made from petroleum, so his transport costs rise when its price rises.
Why does the building have a smoke detector in every room?
Roasting produces a great deal of smoke.
What method does Omar recommend for coffee at home?
He recommends drip coffee, in which hot water passes slowly through ground coffee in a paper filter.

lessons.title: A Sign for a Garden Shop
lessons.summary: A brother and sister who open a garden shop work out, with a designer's help, how the shop should look.
lessons.text:
When Grace Miller and her brother Tom opened a small garden shop, they spent more time arguing about the sign than about anything else. Their arguments, looking back, taught them a good deal about how a small business presents itself to the world.

The shop sells what a city gardener needs: seeds, flower bulbs, small trees, pots and house plants. Grace's favorite corner is the moss table, covered in soft green moss, stones and tiny plants, which customers can buy in glass bowls. Moss needs little light and little care, so it suits people with small apartments.

The first argument was about the font. Grace wanted a curving font that looked like handwriting, with long, elegant letters. Tom thought it looked too feminine and worried that it might keep some customers away. Grace replied that most of their customers would probably be women, and that a feminine look was nothing to apologize for. In the end, they asked a designer for help. She explained that a font should, above all, be easy to read from across the street, and that thin, curving letters fail that test, whatever their style. They chose a simple, rounded font that neither of them had first suggested.

The second argument was about the shape of the sign. The space above the shop window is long and narrow, so the designer proposed a horizontal sign, wide rather than tall. A horizontal sign, she added, also matches the way people walk: their eyes move along the street, not up and down. Beneath the shop's name, she drew a small flower bulb with a green shoot. The bulb became their logo, because a bulb looks like nothing much in the fall and becomes a flower in the spring, which is, Grace says, exactly what a new business hopes to do.

The third question was the website and social media. Here, the brother and sister agreed quickly. Every photo would show one plant and come with a short, useful caption: its name, how much light it needs and how often to water it. Tom wrote the first hundred captions himself. A good caption, he learned, answers the question a customer would ask in the shop.

Some products needed more explanation than others. Aloe plants sold slowly until Grace wrote a caption explaining that the clear gel inside the leaves can calm a small burn. After that, customers asked about the gel so often that she put a small card beside the plants with the same words.

A year later, the sign still hangs above the window, the bulb is printed on every paper bag, and the moss bowls sell out every December. Grace and Tom still argue, but now mostly about plants.

Questions:
What does the shop sell?
It sells seeds, flower bulbs, small trees, pots and house plants.
Why did Tom dislike Grace's first font?
He thought it looked too feminine and might keep some customers away.
Why did the designer propose a horizontal sign?
The space above the window is long and narrow, and people's eyes move along the street.
Why did the bulb become the shop's logo?
A bulb looks like nothing much in the fall and becomes a flower in the spring, as a new business hopes to do.
What does each caption include?
Each caption gives the plant's name, how much light it needs and how often to water it.
